extracted.intended_audience: educators, university administrators, students, and readers interested in the theory and purpose of higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards about the aim, content, and character of a university/liberal education — what intellectual ‘enlargement’ is, how it differs from mere acquirement, and what a liberal education should produce in a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: University's object: intellectual culture
rubrics_metrics.description: A university, in its bare idea, has as its direct scope the cultivation of the intellect — to educate the intellect to reason well in all matters, to reach out towards truth, and to grasp it. It 'contemplates neither moral impression nor mechanical production' but 'intellectual culture' as its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by analogy (hospital heals, gymnasium exercises limbs). The university's mission is distinct from training for particular arts, duties, or professions; its work is to form the intellect itself. This is foundational: other aims (moral formation, professional training, state or church uses) are secondary or external to this essential function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a liberal education (ideal outcome in a person)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man has had a liberal education who has: his body the ready servant of his will; an intellect like a clear, cold logical engine with all parts of equal strength; a mind stored with fundamental truths and laws of Nature; passions trained by a vigorous will and tender conscience; a cultivated love of beauty, hatred of vileness, and respect for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage lists balanced physical, intellectual, moral, and aesthetic qualities as constituent parts of the 'liberal' ideal. Use this composite as a checklist for the intended character and capacities a liberal education should produce, not merely a list of courses or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial education should anticipate natural education
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial (man-made) education ought to prepare the child to receive Nature's education — to prevent incapacity, ignorance, or wilful disobedience, and to enable the pupil to perceive Nature's rewards without needing the painful penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education's role is corrective and preparatory relative to 'Nature's harsh' discipline. The objective is to make students ready to benefit from natural consequences rather than suffer them; curricula and pedagogy should be designed as anticipatory training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (acquirements) is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiring facts, memory, and wide information are indispensable conditions of intellectual enlargement but do not constitute the whole of liberal education; knowledge is a means, not the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman emphasizes that mere accumulation (memory, lists of facts, wide reading) without transformation does not equal 'philosophy' or true culture. Examples of anti-patterns: clever boys who only store facts, learned antiquarians, annalists, naturalists with no systematic insight. Evaluate whether knowledge has been 'digested' and related, not just amassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlargement = active formative process (digestion and systematising)
rubrics_metrics.description: True enlargement consists in the mind's energetic action on new ideas — forming, ordering, and making received knowledge subjectively one's own; in short, digestion and systematising of ideas so they cohere within the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: ability to compare ideas, refer new learning to prior knowledge, form a connected view, and see relations among matters. Positive examples: the transformative effect of astronomy, travel, and history when they lead to new centres of thought. Anti-patterns: passive accumulation where disparate facts leave the mind where it was.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual perfection requires grasp of relations and principles (generalisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To improve the intellect one must 'ascend' above mere particulars — generalise, reduce to method, grasp principles, and group acquisitions by them; to command a field is to mount above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: teaching and curriculum should cultivate generalisation and principled understanding, not only detail. Newman warns against being 'under' one’s knowledge (overwhelmed by facts) and recommends training that enables students to wield knowledge rather than be tyrannised by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer depth and grounding over superficial breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern error is distracting the mind with a profusion of subjects producing smattering instead of real enlargement — 'a smattering of a hundred things or a memory for detail, is not a philosophical or comprehensive view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula should avoid encouraging superficial acquaintance with many disciplines in lieu of thorough acquisition of some. Newman critiques the notion that attendance, membership, or passive exposure equals education. Use measures of depth (mastery, systematic understanding) rather than mere breadth or exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory is valuable but must be subordinate to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and ready memory is a real treasure, but memory can 'tyrannise' the intellect, producing passive, uncontrolled succession of ideas; memory without reason leads to a mind without initiation or true control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess learners for the ability to think while knowing (control, initiation, synthesis) rather than only recall. Watch for signs of being carried along by associative trains of thought or excessive dependence on memory at the expense of analytic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: University education distinct from professional or moral training
rubrics_metrics.description: The university's office is not to produce expert practical skills or enforce moral impressions — it 'professes to exercise the mind neither in art nor in duty' but in intellectual culture; professional knowledge and moral/religious instruction are related questions to be considered separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating university programmes, distinguish components aiming at pure intellectual culture (philosophical habit of mind) from vocational or doctrinal training. Both have value, but the university's primary standard should be whether it cultivates reason and philosophical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of a cultured intellect: calm, comprehensive, impartial, self-possessed
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly trained intellect is 'patient, collected, and majestically calm,' able to view many things at once as one whole, discern ends and origins, and be free from littleness and prejudice; it is not feverish or partial to a single object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use behavioural and intellectual markers (tolerance of complexity, steadiness under challenge, capacity for synthesis, lack of prejudice) as evidence of true intellectual culture. Contrast with geniuses or heroic spontaneity (natural gifts) which are not the target of institutional education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different sources of enlargement have different characters (science/history/travel vs religion vs unbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlargement can arise from various experiences: scientific or historical study and travel produce exhilaration and widening of horizon; unbelief may produce tumults and intoxicating 'enlargement' leading to moral ruin; religion produces a peaceful and ordered enlargement focused on meaning and moral seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of intellectual growth should consider origin and character of enlargement: whether it leads to ordered, systematic insight and moral steadiness (desirable) or to mere intoxication, superstition, or moral laxity (undesirable).
